theme: The Twelve sent; “Come to me, all who are weary”
readingInstruction: Read Matthew 10:1-11:30. Jesus sends out the Twelve and warns them about opposition. Then John the Baptist sends a question from prison, and Jesus ends the chapter with one of the most beloved invitations in the Bible. Read 11:28-30 slowly.
settingTheScene: Having shown his compassion for the harassed crowds, Jesus calls twelve disciples and sends them to the lost sheep of Israel. The twelve apostles echo the twelve tribes: Jesus is gathering a renewed Israel. His instructions are honest about the cost. Then, in chapter 11, we see doubt and rejection, and Jesus responds with an invitation to the weary.
observation: “And he called to him his twelve disciples and gave them authority over unclean spirits” (10:1).
“These twelve Jesus sent out, instructing them, Go nowhere among the Gentiles and enter no town of the Samaritans, but go rather to the lost sheep of the house of Israel” (10:5-6).
“Behold, I am sending you out as sheep in the midst of wolves, so be wise as serpents and innocent as doves” (10:16).
“Whoever loves father or mother more than me is not worthy of me” (10:37).
“Whoever finds his life will lose it, and whoever loses his life for my sake will find it” (10:39).
“Are you the one who is to come, or shall we look for another?” (11:3).
“Come to me, all who labor and are heavy laden, and I will give you rest” (11:28).
“For my yoke is easy, and my burden is light” (11:30).
interpretation:
The commission is clear and costly. The disciples are to proclaim the kingdom, heal, and cast out demons, depending on others for hospitality. Jesus warns them that they will be hated, brought before governors, and divided from their families. Yet he repeats, “Do not be afraid,” because the Father who cares for the sparrows cares for them. Those who acknowledge him before people, he will acknowledge before his Father.

His words about family are hard: loving him above father and mother. This is not a call to hate one’s family, but a statement that he must come first. And the paradox: finding your life means losing it for his sake.

Then John the Baptist, in prison, sends a question. He had announced the coming judge, and now he is in a cell, and Jesus is healing and eating with sinners. He wonders, “Are you the one?” It is a very human doubt. Jesus does not rebuke him. He points to the works: the blind see, the lame walk, lepers are cleansed, the poor have good news. And he says, “Blessed is the one who is not offended by me.” He then praises John as the greatest of the prophets.

Jesus condemns the cities that saw miracles and did not repent. And then, to the surprise of the reader, he prays and offers an invitation. “Come to me, all who labor and are heavy laden.” The yoke is the picture of a teacher’s way of life. The Pharisees’ yoke was heavy with rules. Jesus’ yoke is gentle. His rest is not a break from work but a relationship in which he carries the weight with us.
connection: Jeremiah 31:25 promises to satisfy the weary soul. Exodus 33:14 records God saying, “My presence will go with you, and I will give you rest.” Acts 15:10 calls the burden of the law a yoke that neither we nor our fathers could bear. Hebrews 4:9-11 speaks of a Sabbath rest for the people of God. Luke 14:26-33 teaches the cost of discipleship. Philippians 3:7-8 shows Paul counting all things as loss for Christ. 1 John 5:3: his commandments are not burdensome.
application:
If you are weary today, stop and take Jesus’ invitation personally. Tell him specifically what is heavy.

Think of a person who is doubting. Respond like Jesus did to John: patiently, with evidence of God’s goodness.

Ask what it means to take his yoke and learn from him. What practice could you begin?
prayerPrompts: Come to Jesus weary and burdened, and tell him what weighs on you.
Ask him to teach you, for he is gentle and lowly in heart.
Take his yoke, and tell him what that means.
